title: The year
hook: zakat is due when wealth has been held a full lunar year

segments.voice: Yesterday, two and a half percent, and your line: one in forty. Did you find a fortieth of anything in your head, by ten and then by four? Today, the clock that zakat runs on. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

On the evening the new moon is first seen, someone in the family steps outside, looks low on the horizon, and finds it: a thin silver line, barely there. A month has begun. Muslims have watched for that line for the start of Ramadan and the days of Hajj. It also turns out to be the clock for something less famous. Money in a savings account doesn't announce when zakat is due on it. There's no bill in the mail. The only reminder is the moon going around, month after month, until a whole year of moons has passed over what you hold. The word for that year is today's word: hawl.
screen: `A THIN SILVER LINE AT DUSK.` → `A MONTH HAS BEGUN.` → `A YEAR OF MOONS: HAWL.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, with a similar one in at-Tirmidhi, says that no zakat is due on wealth until the hawl, the year, has passed over it. Wealth has to stay with you for a full year before it's counted. Money that arrives and leaves in a season isn't. Second, which year. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "the number of the months with Allah is twelve months", and elsewhere calls the new moons fixed times for people. The Islamic calendar follows those moons. So zakat's year is a year of moons, and because the moon's year and the sun's year don't line up, a zakat date fixed by the moon slides earlier on a wall calendar from one year to the next. Third, the exception. A harvest doesn't wait for a year. The Qur'an tells farmers to give the due of their crops on the day of the harvest. Wealth that comes all at once out of the ground is shared when it comes, and a later day on this path is about that harvest. Fourth, the date itself. Some Muslims set their zakat date to the day their wealth first crossed the threshold, and count a year of moons from there. Some choose a day in Ramadan, so their giving falls in that month. And the schools of law differ on what happens if savings dip below the line partway through the year, so people ask a scholar they trust. What these answers share is a date: one day a year when the whole of what you hold gets looked at, honestly, and a share goes out.
screen: `NOT DUE UNTIL A YEAR PASSES.` · `A YEAR OF MOONS.` · `THE HARVEST DOESN'T WAIT.` · `ONE DAY A YEAR, CHOSEN.` · then, large: `THE NUMBER OF THE MONTHS WITH ALLAH IS TWELVE MONTHS.`

segments.voice: The practice: pick your zakat date, or, if zakat isn't yours to pay, pick a yearly date for looking honestly at what you have. Settle, and breathe. Let a few candidates come up: a day in Ramadan, the start of a new year, a birthday, the day your savings first grew. Don't choose quickly. Breathe in with one, out with another, and see which one feels like a day you'd actually keep. When one stays, let it stay. The bell holds the time.
Hawl. The year that wealth must be held before zakat is due, counted in moons. Today's word.
Your line: a yearly date. Today, write the date you chose somewhere you'll see it again, a calendar or a note on your phone. Tomorrow: gold, trade, crops and herds. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims who pay zakat keep a yearly zakat date by the Islamic lunar calendar, some fixing it in Ramadan, and on that day total their zakatable wealth above the nisab.

fork.setup: you're a farmer. your grain comes in this week. you think: I'll wait a year and pay zakat on it with my savings. what does the Qur'an say?
options: wait the full year, like savings.
give its due on the day of the harvest.
fork.reveal: give the due on the harvest day. the harvest doesn't wait for the hawl.

original.note: Arabic: the year that must pass over wealth before zakat is due.

trapdoor: what you thought: zakat is due whenever you feel like giving.
what it means: savings above the line are counted once a year, after a full year of moons has passed over them.
what a scholar hears: the hawl applies to savings, gold and trade goods; the harvest is due on reaping, and the schools differ on mid-year dips below the nisab.
recall: asking God to choose the good

notes: Pickthall 9:36 quoted from memory (his text opens 'Lo! the number of the months with Allah is twelve months'); confirm.
Abu Dawud 1573 and Tirmidhi 631 for the hawl: confirm numbers and gradings.
2:189 (new moons as fixed times) and 6:141 (due on the harvest day) paraphrased.
The voice says the moon's year and sun's year don't line up without giving the day count (claims rule).
Zakat-date practices (first crossing of nisab; Ramadan) are described with 'some'; the schools' positions on a mid-year dip below nisab are left general. Confirm.
The hook's family scene of moon-sighting is a general picture, not a sourced claim about any community.
